Belgium is not working well... and it is once again the European Commission that is telling it this.

The Commission recommends that Belgium invest much more in education and infrastructure to increase its economic potential.

But it turns out that all these skills are fragmented in our country: education depends on communities and public works in the regions. The rest is in line.

Moreover, the Commission does not hesitate to point this out: our institutional apparatus is inefficient! Successive state reforms have completely stifled the country and each government now has only the end of its legislature as its only horizon.

Prohibitive

Belgian federalism is unique in the world and is characterised by a phenomenon of "deconstruction". Where, in general, countries or regions join forces to "do better together", here at home, partners dissociate themselves, hoping to "do better alone in their own corner".

The current federal Belgium suffers from three original design flaws, which makes the system increasingly difficult to operate:

  • The model developed without choosing between a community-oriented federalism (the Flemish option) and a region-based federalism (the Walloon option and then also Brussels); as long as there were few competences to allocate, this was not too serious, it is now a major handicap.
  • There is no "hierarchy of norms", in other words, there is no leader/parliament/government that ultimately decides. No government can dictate its conduct to another. Everything is supposed to be taken "in consultation" but nothing is provided for in the event of failure of this consultation.
  • Belgium has become the only federal democracy where there are no longer any national parties, unlike Switzerland or Canada in particular. Everyone is therefore only responsible for "his" part of the population.

The Commission notes this inertia and inefficiency. Everything is going too slowly for us, current expenses are too high and investments are insufficient.

Unaffordable federalism

In fact, our unravelling federalism is simply overpriced and ineffective. The structure has become an incomprehensible... and unmanageable monster. Reforms are becoming impossible. In particular, Europe points to our overly generous company car system or a labour market that is not sufficiently open to workers of foreign origin. These observations are repeated year after year and successive governments have not been able to find a solution.

The current electoral campaign should constitute a collective awareness of these shortcomings and the remedies to be applied. However, special interests or short-sighted policies may well remain the only political horizon.
